evidence.span: We have demonstrated a broadly applicable approach to align, error-correct, group, and count sequences from orthogonal barcodes to quantify multimodal data such as cell surface protein abundance, to demultiplex samples, and to perform large-scale perturbation experiments. Our approach is fast, memory efficient, and extensible: orthogonal barcode quantifications can be obtained for numerous assays with variable sequence structure such the recently developed spatial RNA-seq assays (Srivatsan et al. 2021) and massively parallel reporter assays (Gordon et al. 2020). This allows future assay developers to avoid producing, validating, and maintaining software implementing ad hoc solutions. Moreover, some current methods are slow, have high memory requirements, and are specifically tailored for specific assays, which can result in batch effects when performing integrative analysis. Methods such as CITE-seq-Count offer extensibility features for different barcode strategies, but are slow and memory-intensive. The speed and efficiency of our approach enables reproducible single-cell analysis in the cloud with tools such as Google Colab. We anticipate that our framework for quantifying orthogonal barcoding assays will be useful as multimodal assays proliferate (Packer and Trapnell 2018), and that our quality control tool will help assay developers avoid pitfalls in barcode design and help practitioners quality control orthogonal barcode assays. Finally, while our approach is currently engineered to correct mismatch errors, robustness to other types of sequencing errors are possible via other methods that could readily be incorporated in our modular framework (Zorita, Cuscó, and Filion 2015; Booeshaghi et al. 2020; Milo S. Johnson, Sandeep Venkataram, Sergey Kryazhimskiy 2022).

evidence.span: Standard single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis (scRNA-seq) workflows consist of converting raw read data into cell-gene count matrices through sequence alignment, followed by anal- yses including filtering, highly variable gene selection, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and differential expression analysis. Seurat and Scanpy are the most widely-used packages implementing such workflows, and are generally thought to implement individual steps sim- ilarly. We investigate in detail the algorithms and methods underlying Seurat and Scanpy and find that there are, in fact, considerable differences in the outputs of Seurat and Scanpy. The extent of differences between the programs is approximately equivalent to the variabil- ity that would be introduced in benchmarking scRNA-seq datasets by sequencing less than 5% of the reads or analyzing less than 20% of the cell population. Additionally, distinct versions of Seurat and Scanpy can produce very different results, especially during parts of differential expression analysis. Our analysis highlights the need for users of scRNA-seq to carefully assess the tools on which they rely, and the importance of developers of scientific software to prioritize transparency, consistency, and reproducibility for their tools.

object.description: Large single-cell atlases depend on comparing datasets generated by many assays, so preprocessing must be consistent before biological interpretation begins. relations.statement: This publication contains this grounded claim.

evidence.span: A frequent refrain in single-cell genomics is that "uniform processing" of data is desirable and important. However when contrasted against the large number of single-cell genomics assays (Klein et al. 2015; Hagemann-Jensen et al. 2020; Zheng et al. 2017; Rosenberg et al. 2018; W. Xu et al. 2022; Gehring et al. 2020; Stoeckius et al. 2017; Schraivogel et al. 2020), and given that ideally analysis methods should be optimized and tailored for the assays to which they will be applied, the question arises why is uniform processing desirable? For example, in the case of single-cell RNA-seq it may be interesting to study cell-type isoform specificity (Booeshaghi et al. 2021), whereas for single-cell ATAC-seq the notion of isoforms is meaningless because the assay is based on genomic DNA, not cDNA, sequencing (Cusanovich et al. 2015). The reason uniform preprocessing can be important, is that with increasing amounts of data being generated (Svensson, da Veiga Beltrame, and Pachter 2020), datasets are seldom analyzed in isolation, and to the extent possible, it is desirable to avoid batch effects resulting from assay- or data-specific methods. Thus, uniform processing is increasingly intended to mean uniform preprocessing1 of data so that meta-analyses can be shielded from batch effects (Zhang et al. 2021; Davis et al. 2018).

object.label: Design principles for open source bioinstrumentation: the poseidon syringe pump system as an example
object.description: Rapidly changing single-cell genomics benefits from adaptable laboratory hardware, while shared open designs can keep instrument developers from starting from scratch. Open bioinstruments still need concrete design guidance to remain functional, robust, simple, modular, benchmarked, and documented. Poseidon demonstrates these principles with a customizable syringe-pump and microscope system that costs under $400, assembles in under an hour, and performs microfluidic experiments.

object.label: Low-cost, scalable, and automated fluid sampling for fluidics applications
object.description: Automated microfluidic-stream fraction collection is preferable to tedious, error-prone manual collection. Commercial fraction collectors are often expensive and hard to customize, while existing open-source collectors can remain complex and difficult to source or manufacture. Colosseum is a low-cost, modular, one-motor automated fraction collector that can be built from off-the-shelf and 3D-printed components, assembled quickly, and used for accurate fraction collection across a wide flow-rate range.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Low-cost, scalable, and automated fluid sampling for fluidics applications.

object.label: Modular, efficient and constant-memory single-cell RNA-seq preprocessing
object.description: Single-cell RNA-seq preprocessing quantifies transcript or gene abundance in individual cells. Experiments can span 10^6 to 10^10 reads, while existing workflows can require extensive time and disk space or memory that grows with dataset size. kallisto-bustools achieves near-optimal speed, constant memory, scaling to arbitrarily large datasets, Cell Ranger-consistent downstream analyses, and fast RNA-velocity analysis.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Modular, efficient and constant-memory single-cell RNA-seq preprocessing.

object.label: Principles of open source bioinstrumentation applied to the poseidon syringe pump system
object.description: Open bioinstrumentation can lower costs and let laboratories adapt hardware to fast-changing biological experiments. Adoption is limited when designs are hard to build, unsafe, poorly documented, or insufficiently benchmarked. The sub-$400 Poseidon syringe pump and microscope system demonstrates functional, robust, safe, simple, modular, benchmarked, and documented open bioinstrumentation.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Principles of open source bioinstrumentation applied to the poseidon syringe pump system.

object.label: Quantifying orthogonal barcodes for sequence census assays
object.description: Barcode-based sequence census assays can label biological features, but barcode design and technical noise complicate quantification. Assay-specific tools can be slow, memory-intensive, and hard to standardize across multimodal, multiplexing, and perturbation assays. kITE uniformly quantifies orthogonal barcode assays with fast, memory-efficient kallisto-bustools processing, while qcbc evaluates barcode-set quality and identifies ambiguity from shared subsequences, homopolymers, and low-diversity designs.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Quantifying orthogonal barcodes for sequence census assays.

object.label: Quantifying orthogonal barcodes for sequence census assays
object.description: Orthogonal barcodes encode biological and technical information across multimodal, multiplexing, and perturbation assays. Barcode quantification is complicated by design and technical noise, while assay-specific tools can be slow, memory-intensive, and introduce batch effects. kITE quantifies diverse barcode assays with high agreement and lower runtime and memory than comparators, while qcbc detects shared subsequences responsible for improper quantification.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Quantifying orthogonal barcodes for sequence census assays.

object.label: Reliable and accurate diagnostics from highly multiplexed sequencing assays
object.description: Scalable, inexpensive, and secure SARS-CoV-2 testing is crucial for pandemic control, and highly multiplexed sequencing assays are promising alternatives to RT-qPCR tests. Their clinical use requires reliable analysis, interpretation, and computational workflows that handle sample indices, biological targets, gene counts, and infection-status classification. A kallisto-bustools workflow processes recently proposed sequencing-based diagnostic tests quickly and with low memory, validates SwabSeq analysis against an orthogonal workflow, and extends to assays with different targets and sample-index structures.

relations.statement: Jase Gehring is an author of Reliable and accurate diagnostics from highly multiplexed sequencing assays.
